opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a good question, because when I finished my PhD I was at a bit of a crossroads. A lot of my doctoral work was on understanding the latent space of generative models: how a GAN actually encodes concepts like pose, age, or lighting, and whether you could find directions in that space that let you edit an image in a controllable, interpretable way. Academically that was exciting, but I kept asking myself whether these ideas would hold up outside carefully curated benchmarks.

What appealed to me about going into industry, and a company like ByteDance in particular, was the closeness to real users. When you work on image editing in a lab, your "user" is basically a test set and a few metrics. In a company whose products are built around creation (people making videos, applying effects, retouching photos), you immediately see what people actually want to do, and it's often quite different from what researchers assume. People don't care whether your FID improved by half a point. They care whether the edit looks natural, whether it preserves their identity, whether it runs fast enough on their phone.

There's also the practical side: data and compute. Generative modeling, even then, was becoming very resource-hungry, and having the infrastructure to train at scale changes which questions you can even ask.

That said, I don't want to paint it as purely rosy. There's a real tension between doing research that's forward-looking and research that ships next quarter. Part of what I had to learn was how to protect some space for longer-term exploration, the kind of work that might not pay off for a year, while still staying connected to product needs. I think the best outcomes came when those two fed each other: a product problem exposed a gap in our understanding, and solving it properly turned out to be a genuinely interesting research question.

So overall I found it a very stimulating environment. It pushed me to think less about "can we edit an image in latent space" and more about "what does controllable generation really mean for ordinary people," and that shift in perspective has stayed with me ever since.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a very different environment from the lab, and that was exactly what I needed at that stage. During my PhD at CUHK I spent most of my time on GAN latent spaces, understanding what the generator had actually learned and how to steer it. That was very satisfying intellectually, but the gap between a nice interpretability result and something a real person would use to edit a photo was enormous. At ByteDance that gap was the whole job.

The first thing I noticed was the scale and the proximity to real users. You have products like Douyin and CapCut where editing is not a demo, it is something hundreds of millions of people touch every day. So the questions changed. Instead of asking whether a method can move a semantic direction in latent space, you ask whether it works on a blurry phone photo of someone's grandmother, whether it runs fast enough on a mobile chip, and whether a user understands what they got. Those constraints were frustrating at first, but they forced a lot of honesty about which ideas were real.

The second thing was the people. The research group there, under Jiaya Jia and later around the generative model team, had a mix of very strong academic researchers and very good engineers, and the line between them was quite blurry. I learned a lot about data from engineers who had never written a paper. That mix is hard to get in a university.

And third, I would say ByteDance was unusually willing to let the generative work stay somewhat exploratory. The shift from GANs to diffusion was happening right around then, and I was allowed to spend real time on foundational questions about controllability and image priors rather than only shipping features. Not every company would have tolerated that. So for me it was a good bridge: close enough to products to keep me grounded, open enough that I could keep doing research I cared about, and eventually that is also what made me comfortable moving on to build something more ambitious at Ant Group.

astra-6.text: For me, the appeal was the chance to connect image-editing research with practical applications. During a PhD, you can focus quite deeply on a particular research question. In an industry setting, you also have to ask whether the method is useful and whether people can actually control it. That connection between research and practical use was what interested me about pursuing this work at ByteDance.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the appeal was the connection between research and real applications. With image editing, you can have an interesting technical result, but you also want to understand whether it gives people the control they actually need. I saw ByteDance as an opportunity to explore that connection—to keep working on research questions while thinking more seriously about how people would use the results.
